nature_note: Poverty Point, the largest settlement of its age in North America, stands on Macon Ridge overlooking the Mississippi floodplain. The ridge would have stayed dry in floods while fish, turtles, deer and nuts lay close by. Archaeologists infer gatherings from the earthworks; no sound survives.
sources: 64 Parishes, Poverty Point <https://64parishes.org/entry/poverty-point>

nature_note: Instruments come from each nation's own country, and they differ. Chitimacha elders in 1933 described a flute cut from cane and a dried alligator skin scraped with a stick. Coushatta women keep stomp dance rhythm with turtle shakers. United Houma Nation songs are about the lands and the waters.
sources: Frances Densmore, A Search for Songs among the Chitimacha Indians in Louisiana, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 133 (1943), full text <https://archive.org/stream/bulletin1331943smit/bulletin1331943smit_djvu.txt> | Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana, Coushatta Powwow <https://coushattapowwow.com/> | Garde Voir Ci (Nicholls State University), The Musical Backdrop by Jade Williams <https://gardevoirci.nicholls.edu/2021/music/>

nature_note: Much of Congo Square's sound was made from what the country supplied: drums of hollowed logs and empty barrels, rattles of gourd, animal jawbones, wooden horns. The dancing happened outdoors, in rings on open common ground at the back edge of the colonial town.
sources: 64 Parishes, Congo Square <https://64parishes.org/entry/congo-square> | 64 Parishes, Congo Square: La Place Publique by Jerah Johnson <https://64parishes.org/congo-square-la-place-publique>

nature_note: Creole music belongs to the families who worked the southwest Louisiana prairies. Today's Creole trail riders include descendants of free people of color and enslaved Africans who managed thousands of cattle there before the Louisiana Purchase, and it was merchants on those prairies who imported the first accordions.
sources: 64 Parishes, Creole Trail Rides by Zella Palmer <https://64parishes.org/creole-trail-rides> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Cajun and Zydeco Music Traditions by Barry Jean Ancelet <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/lt/articles_essays/cajunzydeco.html>

nature_note: Across the Atchafalaya Basin from Baton Rouge lies the prairie homeland of Cajun music, a region that stayed isolated until the oil industry arrived in the early twentieth century. In its crowded, unamplified dance halls the air-driven accordion and a high, piercing singing style carried over the noise of the dancers.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, The Treasured Traditions of Louisiana Music by Ben Sandmel <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/treas_trad_la_music.html> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Cajun and Zydeco Music Traditions by Barry Jean Ancelet <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/lt/articles_essays/cajunzydeco.html>

nature_note: Zydeco takes its name from the farm. Creoles trace the word to les haricots, snap beans, in the saying that the beans aren't salty, and it also means hard times. The music still keeps country company at Creole trail rides, where riders dance to zydeco late into the night.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, Cajun and Zydeco Music Traditions by Barry Jean Ancelet <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/lt/articles_essays/cajunzydeco.html> | 64 Parishes, Creole Trail Rides by Zella Palmer <https://64parishes.org/creole-trail-rides>

nature_note: Water both hosted and carried early jazz. Bands competed for crowds at resorts and camps built on piers over Lake Pontchartrain, and from 1918 the Streckfus excursion steamers hired New Orleans players, taking their sound up the Mississippi to river cities such as St. Louis, Davenport and St. Paul.
sources: National Park Service, New Orleans Jazz National Historical Park, early jazz history <https://www.nps.gov/jazz/learn/historyculture/history_early.htm> | 64 Parishes, Jazz at the Lakefront by Bruce Boyd Raeburn <https://64parishes.org/jazz-at-the-lakefront> | Tulane University Libraries, Riverboats and Jazz: Fate Marable's New Orleans Band on the S.S. Sidney <https://exhibits.tulane.edu/?p=1149> | Tulane University Libraries, Riverboats and Jazz: The S.S. Sidney <https://exhibits.tulane.edu/?p=1155>

nature_note: Brass band music is made for the open street. Social aid and pleasure clubs parade for miles through neighborhood backstreets on Sunday afternoons in a season that runs from September through May, and funeral processions play dirges on the way to the burial and livelier music afterward.
sources: 64 Parishes, Jazz Funerals and Second Line Parades <https://64parishes.org/entry/jazz-funerals-and-second-line-parades> | 64 Parishes, Brass Bands of New Orleans <https://64parishes.org/entry/brass-bands-of-new-orleans>

nature_note: One account of the tradition's beginnings, offered as a possibility rather than settled fact, is that people escaping slavery found refuge with Houma, Chitimacha and other tribes in the swamplands around New Orleans. Its calendar is fixed: a new suit every Mardi Gras morning, then St. Joseph's night.
sources: 64 Parishes, Mardi Gras Indians <https://64parishes.org/entry/mardi-gras-indians>

nature_note: Louisiana blues changes with the land: a rough-edged rural style in the northeastern parishes, akin to the Mississippi Delta next door, and a relaxed sound around Baton Rouge. Swamp blues is named either for a swamp beside the players' homes or for producer J.D. Miller's wish for a regional label.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, From Rural to Urban, From Acoustic to Amplified: the Blues in Louisiana by Ben Sandmel <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/blues.html> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Blues and Blacks in the Red Stick by Joyce Jackson <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/brblues1.html>

nature_note: In the Mississippi floodplain of northeast Louisiana, old plantation churches kept Easter Rock, an Easter eve vigil said to predate the Civil War. Its sound depends on the building: feet on a wooden floor beat like a drum, and the rockers lament losing that sound on concrete.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, Everyone Rockin' Together: Continuity and Creativity in the Louisiana Delta Easter Rock by Susan Roach <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/easterrock.html>

nature_note: North Louisiana belongs to the upland and riverine South. Its folk culture took shape on farmsteads, plantations and sharecrop land among river bottoms, piney woods and hills. Country music grew from the ballads and fiddle tunes of Anglo-Celtic settlers, and by 1929 a fiddler was recording the driving sound oil field camps wanted.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, The Creole State: An Introduction to Louisiana Traditional Culture by Nicholas R. Spitzer <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/lt/articles_essays/creole_art_creole_state.html> | 64 Parishes, Country Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/country-music>

nature_note: The swamp in swamp pop is an outsider's shorthand for south Louisiana. British writer Bill Millar coined the term around 1970, years after the hits, for music made by Cajun and Black Creole players in Acadiana and southeast Texas. The name points to a homeland, not to a sound.
sources: 64 Parishes, Swamp Pop <https://64parishes.org/entry/swamp-pop> | Louisiana Folklife Program, The Treasured Traditions of Louisiana Music by Ben Sandmel <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/treas_trad_la_music.html>

nature_note: Bounce lyrics name particular schools and housing projects. After Hurricane Katrina in 2005 displaced the people who made the music and the city's public housing was demolished, those songs became a record of places that are no longer there.
sources: 64 Parishes, Bounce <https://64parishes.org/entry/bounce>

nature_note: Hurricane Katrina in 2005 scattered New Orleans rappers and producers to Baton Rouge, Houston, Dallas and Atlanta, where they struggled to keep their careers moving; Lil Wayne relocated to Miami. The storm is the clearest case of the environment redirecting this music.
sources: 64 Parishes, Rap, Hip-Hop and Bounce Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/rap-hip-hop-and-bounce-music>

nature_note: West Carroll Parish lies on Macon Ridge, a wide alluvial terrace veneered with wind-blown silt that overlooks the Mississippi floodplain. The ridge would have stayed dry during floods while giving easy access to bottomland fish, turtles and aquatic roots and to upland deer and nuts.
sources: U.S. EPA and USGS, Summary Table: Characteristics of the Ecoregions of Louisiana (poster back) <https://dmap-prod-oms-edc.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/ORD/Ecoregions/la/la_back.pdf> | 64 Parishes, Poverty Point <https://64parishes.org/entry/poverty-point>

nature_note: Caddo songs carry this country with them. Turkey Dance songs, which must be danced before sunset, recall events such as the creation of Caddo Lake, and a riding song about the removal from Louisiana calls back across the Ouachita River while a redbird warns travelers that daylight is near.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, Caddo Homecoming by Dayna Bowker Lee <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/creole_art_caddo_homecomin.html>

nature_note: The Chitimacha say their lands once took in the entire Atchafalaya Basin, west toward Lafayette, south to the Gulf and east toward New Orleans. River cane, the material of the nation's celebrated basketry, was also the stuff of the flute described to Frances Densmore at Charenton in 1933.
sources: Chitimacha Tribe of Louisiana, Tribal History <https://www.chitimacha.gov/history-culture/tribal-history> | Frances Densmore, A Search for Songs among the Chitimacha Indians in Louisiana, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 133 (1943), full text <https://archive.org/stream/bulletin1331943smit/bulletin1331943smit_djvu.txt>

nature_note: Colonial grants gave each Acadian family a narrow frontage on the nearest waterway, running forty arpents back. Swampy backlands held eastern settlers to the banks of the Mississippi and Bayou Lafourche, while those in the Teche country could, and often did, move out onto the uninhabited prairies beyond.
sources: Acadian Memorial, Acadian Immigration into South Louisiana, 1764-1785 <https://acadianmemorial.org/acadian-immigration-into-south-louisiana-1764-1785/>

nature_note: This was prairie: flat coastal plain of bluestem and switchgrass with gallery forest along the streams, now mostly rice fields and crawfish ponds. Here the courir de Mardi Gras rides from farm to farm, on horseback or trailer, begging a chicken or some rice for the communal gumbo.
sources: U.S. EPA and USGS, Summary Table: Characteristics of the Ecoregions of Louisiana (poster back) <https://dmap-prod-oms-edc.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/ORD/Ecoregions/la/la_back.pdf> | 64 Parishes, Courir de Mardi Gras <https://64parishes.org/entry/courir-de-mardi-gras>

nature_note: Trail rides keep zydeco tied to this country's ranching past. At gatherings in places such as Plaisance and Cecilia, Creole riders whose forebears managed cattle on the southwest Louisiana prairies come together to ride, cook and dance to zydeco into the small hours.
sources: 64 Parishes, Creole Trail Rides by Zella Palmer <https://64parishes.org/creole-trail-rides>

nature_note: Lead Belly's music came out of the cotton country around Shreveport. Born on the Jeter Plantation near Mooringsport, he was known for the prodigious amount of cotton he could pick, and he worked the fields between Shreveport and Dallas, playing weekend gatherings, as well as the saloons of Fannin Street.
sources: 64 Parishes, Huddie Lead Belly Ledbetter <https://64parishes.org/entry/lead-belly> | National Park Service, Huddie William Leadbelly Ledbetter <https://www.nps.gov/locations/lowermsdeltaregion/leadbelly.htm>

nature_note: These parishes lie on the Mississippi's alluvial plain, flat meander-belt and backswamp land where cypress swamp and bottomland hardwoods gave way largely to cotton, soybeans and corn. Their blues is a rough-edged rural style close to that of the neighboring Mississippi Delta, played in juke joints in towns such as Ferriday.
sources: U.S. EPA and USGS, Summary Table: Characteristics of the Ecoregions of Louisiana (poster back) <https://dmap-prod-oms-edc.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/ORD/Ecoregions/la/la_back.pdf> | Louisiana Folklife Program, From Rural to Urban, From Acoustic to Amplified: the Blues in Louisiana by Ben Sandmel <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/blues.html>

nature_note: Swamp blues was made by country people come to town. Players from farming communities around Zachary, Clinton, St. Francisville and Slaughter moved to Baton Rouge for petroleum and chemical plant work, and by Silas Hogan's account jammed on porches overlooking Devil's Swamp near Scotlandville, naming their sound for it.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, Blues and Blacks in the Red Stick by Joyce Jackson <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/brblues1.html>

nature_note: Easter Rock belongs to the old plantation churches of the Mississippi floodplain. It has been documented near Clayton in Concordia Parish and continues near Winnsboro in Franklin Parish, with earlier reports from Ferriday and Lake Providence. Participants say it reaches back before the Civil War.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, Everyone Rockin' Together: Continuity and Creativity in the Louisiana Delta Easter Rock by Susan Roach <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/easterrock.html>

nature_note: North Louisiana was settled mainly by English-speaking Protestant British Americans and African Americans, among river bottoms, piney woods and hills. Oil added a new audience: Hiter Colvin, a fiddler from Dubach, recorded in 1929 the driving sound demanded in the north Louisiana oil field camps.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, The Treasured Traditions of Louisiana Music by Ben Sandmel <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/treas_trad_la_music.html> | Louisiana Folklife Program, The Creole State: An Introduction to Louisiana Traditional Culture by Nicholas R. Spitzer <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/lt/articles_essays/creole_art_creole_state.html> | 64 Parishes, Country Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/country-music>

nature_note: The earthworks stand on Macon Ridge, overlooking the west side of the Mississippi floodplain. The setting offered deer, nuts and fruit from the uplands and fish, turtles and aquatic roots from the bottomlands, and the Mississippi, Ouachita and Arkansas rivers were important for trade with other groups.
sources: 64 Parishes, Poverty Point <https://64parishes.org/entry/poverty-point>

nature_note: The mounds stand beside Old River, which about 2,000 years ago would have been the course of the Mississippi itself, so this ceremonial center was raised on the great river's bank. Sightlines between mounds are reported to mark the rising and setting of the sun and moon.
sources: Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana, article on the Marksville site reposted from NOLA.com <https://www.tunicabiloxi.org/this-archaeological-site-drew-pilgrims-2000-years-ago-now-there-are-big-plans-for-its-future/>

nature_note: At Charenton on Bayou Teche in 1933, Chitimacha elders told Frances Densmore how the cane flute came to a boy who shared deer meat with a disguised deity. Older accounts she cited describe a deerskin stretched over a clay pot and a dried alligator skin scraped with a stick.
sources: Frances Densmore, A Search for Songs among the Chitimacha Indians in Louisiana, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 133 (1943), full text <https://archive.org/stream/bulletin1331943smit/bulletin1331943smit_djvu.txt> | Chitimacha Tribe of Louisiana, Tribal History <https://www.chitimacha.gov/history-culture/tribal-history>

nature_note: The Tunica settled opposite the meeting of the Red and Mississippi rivers, a position commanding trade between the two valleys and New Orleans. The tribe's history names corn as a staple honored in celebrations and rituals; before the present Pow Wow began in 1995, a Green Corn festival was held each summer.
sources: Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana, History <https://www.tunicabiloxi.org/history/> | The Advocate, Celebrating Tunica-Biloxi traditions and culture in Marksville <https://www.theadvocate.com/acadiana/entertainment_life/were-a-family-first-celebrating-tunica-biloxi-traditions-and-culture-in-marksville/article_681cd6ac-16f0-11ef-939a-938e7ae472e4.html>

nature_note: The songs of the United Houma Nation are about the lands and the waters, according to a Nicholls State University feature on the tribe's music. Chief August Creppel describes most as prayer songs, handed down by elders and sung with hand drums and big drums made of hides.
sources: Garde Voir Ci (Nicholls State University), The Musical Backdrop by Jade Williams <https://gardevoirci.nicholls.edu/2021/music/>

nature_note: The Coushatta Tribe describes women stomp dancers wearing turtle shakers, a main source of the dance's music, and a fire whose smoke carries prayers upward through the night. Religious stomp dances belong to the Green Corn Ceremony, held in summer at the height of the new crop season.
sources: Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana, Coushatta Powwow <https://coushattapowwow.com/>

nature_note: The square lay at the back of the colonial town on the edge of the City Commons, with the Carondelet Canal's turning basin on one side bringing boats of produce and seafood. It stayed a simple, open, grassy plain, a market ground as well as a dancing ground.
sources: 64 Parishes, Congo Square: La Place Publique by Jerah Johnson <https://64parishes.org/congo-square-la-place-publique>

nature_note: Isleño décimas are the songs of a marsh fishing people: one mocks a boastful shrimper, another tells a crab fisherman's life. Sara-Ann Harris writes that tides, moon, wind and salinity governed the catch and that hurricane season threatened every August to October. Katrina destroyed Delacroix Island, the old center, in 2005.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, The Evolution of the Isleño Identity by Sara-Ann Harris <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/islenos.html> | 64 Parishes, Isleños <https://64parishes.org/entry/islenos>

nature_note: Milneburg stood over the water: dance pavilions and rented camps on piers along Lake Pontchartrain's south shore, reached from town by the Smokey Mary train. Drummer Paul Barbarin recalled a white band playing two camps away from his own, in honest rivalry. Seawall and landfill work after 1927 erased the shoreline itself.
sources: 64 Parishes, Jazz at the Lakefront by Bruce Boyd Raeburn <https://64parishes.org/jazz-at-the-lakefront>

nature_note: Angola is a prison farm of about 18,000 acres assembled from former plantation land on the Mississippi. Prisoners worked its crops and the river levees, and floods struck in 1903, 1912 and 1922. On this working farm the Lomaxes found Lead Belly in 1933.
sources: 64 Parishes, Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola <https://64parishes.org/entry/louisiana-state-penitentiary-at-angola> | 64 Parishes, Huddie Lead Belly Ledbetter <https://64parishes.org/entry/lead-belly>

nature_note: The studio describes its grounds as 26 acres of pine forests, fields and ponds about 70 miles northeast of New Orleans. This is the pine hill country of the Southeastern Plains, historically longleaf pine forest and now largely forest, pine plantation and pasture.
sources: Studio in the Country, official site <https://studiointhecountry.com/> | U.S. EPA and USGS, Summary Table: Characteristics of the Ecoregions of Louisiana (poster back) <https://dmap-prod-oms-edc.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/ORD/Ecoregions/la/la_back.pdf>

nature_note: After Hurricane Katrina in 2005, Fats Domino was rescued by boat from this Lower Ninth Ward house, in the neighborhood where he was raised and chose to remain. A 2006 album that followed was taken as a sign of New Orleans's determination to come back.
sources: Louisiana Office of Tourism, Fats Domino's House <https://www.explorelouisiana.com/music/fats-dominos-house>

nature_note: Mamou is one of the prairie communities where the courir de Mardi Gras runs. Riders on horseback or tractor-drawn trailers call on neighbors across the countryside, chase live chickens and gather rice, sausage and onions for a communal gumbo, singing a song that asks for charity.
sources: 64 Parishes, Courir de Mardi Gras <https://64parishes.org/entry/courir-de-mardi-gras>

nature_note: The 193 Acadians sent to the Attakapas in February 1765 came to a frontier of bayous backed by open prairie. Land was granted in narrow strips fronting the nearest waterway, and settlers who wanted distance from quarrelsome neighbors could, and many did, move onto the uninhabited prairies.
sources: Acadian Memorial, Acadian Immigration into South Louisiana, 1764-1785 <https://acadianmemorial.org/acadian-immigration-into-south-louisiana-1764-1785/>
